title: CastleRat Delivery Chain
subtitle: A fake CAPTCHA paste pulls a scheduled task over SMB and ends in a CastleRat implant that finds its C2 in a Steam profile name.

nodes.label: Fake CAPTCHA paste
nodes.sub: Win+R one-liner dressed up as CAPTCHA text
nodes.desc: The paste stored guest creds for an attacker SMB share and created a scheduled task from an XML file on that share. A trailing REM I am not a robot comment made it look like CAPTCHA text.
nodes.notes: High: the command survived in endpoint telemetry. The lure page itself wasn't preserved.

nodes.label: Task from an SMB share
nodes.sub: cmdkey, then schtasks /XML from a UNC path
nodes.desc: The task, Lowks, is created from full.xml on the attacker's share. Keeping the task on the share lets the operator change what it runs without touching the lure.

nodes.label: Junk-padded stager
nodes.sub: Hundreds of dead lines around one real function
nodes.desc: The task pulls a PowerShell stager. It's mostly hundreds of lines of dead code to dilute AMSI, with one real function that downloads maestrovsd.exe, a .NET loader of about 150 KB.
nodes.notes: The variable names look randomized per deployment, so don't hunt on them.

nodes.label: Brings its own Python
nodes.desc: The loader fetches full signed Python runtimes (3.9 and 3.13) plus install.pyc and melody.pyc, so the process tree shows a trusted pythonw.exe running attacker bytecode. The Python is PyArmor-protected, so static analysis of the .pyc files went nowhere.

nodes.label: UAC bypass
nodes.desc: pythonw.exe spawned ComputerDefaults.exe at High integrity, which fits the ms-settings handler hijack.
nodes.notes: High on the process chain. I treated the registry rewrite as part of the technique rather than something I observed on its own.

nodes.label: Steam dead drop
nodes.sub: C2 read from a Steam profile name, in plain text
nodes.desc: The implant doesn't hardcode its C2. It fetches a Steam Community profile and reads the C2 straight out of the profile name. Steam traffic rarely gets blocked, and swapping infrastructure is just editing a profile. Config extraction also gave an RC4 key that decrypts two more in-memory stages.
nodes.notes: Family is Medium confidence: it rests on the sandbox verdict, YARA hits and infrastructure overlap, not a code comparison.

nodes.label: Stealer and RAT
nodes.desc: Once it's up, it's a full stealer: Chrome, Edge and Firefox data, a long list of crypto wallets and wallet extensions, 1Password and NordPass directories, VPN configs, FTP clients, and screenshots.
